# What AWS credentials the library redacts, and what it leaves alone.
#
# Every key here is built from the ordered run 0123456789ABCDEF, which no real
# credential is. That run is sixteen characters and so is a whole key body, and
# it carries 0, 1, 8 and 9 — the four digits missing from the base32 alphabet
# issued keys are reported to be drawn from. So every key below is one this
# library locates and, if that report is right, no generator would produce.
# That is the pattern's alphabet decision written into the data: it admits
# every character AWS has shown in a key rather than the narrower set other
# people have read off issued ones.

patterns: aws-access-key-id

# The two prefixes AWS documents for an access key ID. AKIA belongs to an IAM
# user or to the account root user and does not expire; ASIA is issued by AWS
# STS along with a session token and does. Each is stated once rather than being
# assumed to follow from the other.

case: a long term access key id in an environment assignment
in:   AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIA0123456789ABCDEF
out:  AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=«aws-access-key-id»

case: a temporary access key id from sts
in:   ASIA0123456789ABCDEF
out:  «aws-access-key-id»

case: an access key id in a shared credentials file
in:   [default]\naws_access_key_id = AKIA0123456789ABCDEF
out:  [default]\naws_access_key_id = «aws-access-key-id»

case: an access key id in the json sts writes
in:   {"AccessKeyId":"ASIA0123456789ABCDEF","Expiration":"2026-08-17T00:00:00Z"}
out:  {"AccessKeyId":"«aws-access-key-id»","Expiration":"2026-08-17T00:00:00Z"}

case: an access key id on a command line
in:   aws sts get-access-key-info --access-key-id AKIA0123456789ABCDEF
out:  aws sts get-access-key-info --access-key-id «aws-access-key-id»

# The lengths either side of twenty. AWS states no length for an access key ID
# anywhere the pattern's author could find; what it states is the AccessKeyId
# field of the IAM and STS APIs, sixteen to a hundred and twenty-eight
# characters — and the pattern's own file says why that is read as the API's
# input filter rather than as the format. Twenty is what every access key ID in
# AWS's documentation is. Unlike the GitHub bodies, which are the shortest
# seen and so a floor, it is used here as a count: nineteen characters are not
# a key, and twenty-four are a key and four
# characters that belong to no credential. The second of those is the price of
# having no boundary behind the match, and the case below is where it is
# written down — a boundary there would drop this key rather than trim it, and
# a real key written against an uppercase letter would come through whole.

case: a body of sixteen characters is a key
in:   AKIA0123456789ABCDEF
out:  «aws-access-key-id»

case: a body of fifteen characters is not
in:   AKIA0123456789ABCDE
out:  AKIA0123456789ABCDE

case: an alphabet run longer than a key is a key and what follows it
in:   AKIA0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ
out:  «aws-access-key-id»GHIJ

# What a key may be written against. The prefix is the whole of the anchor and
# there is no boundary on either side of it, so a key keeps its span whatever
# word character it abuts.

case: an access key id after an underscore
in:   AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID_AKIA0123456789ABCDEF
out:  AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID_«aws-access-key-id»

case: an access key id after a letter
in:   xAKIA0123456789ABCDEF
out:  x«aws-access-key-id»

case: an access key id before an underscore
in:   AKIA0123456789ABCDEF_x
out:  «aws-access-key-id»_x

# Two keys written together. The A that closes ASIA is the A that opens AKIA
# three characters along, so a key can begin inside the span of the one before
# it; the two spans overlap and are redacted as one. Written without that
# overlap the two are separate values, and both go.

case: a key beginning inside the key before it
in:   ASIAKIA0123456789ABCDEF
out:  «aws-access-key-id»

case: two keys with nothing between them
in:   AKIA0123456789ABCDEFASIA0123456789ABCDEF
out:  «aws-access-key-id»«aws-access-key-id»

# Punctuation ends a key, so nothing written after one joins it.

case: an access key id before a host name
in:   host=AKIA0123456789ABCDEF.example.com
out:  host=«aws-access-key-id».example.com

case: an access key id at the end of a sentence
in:   the key is AKIA0123456789ABCDEF.
out:  the key is «aws-access-key-id».

# What this pattern redacts that nobody issued. ASIA is an English word where
# AKIA is not, so an unbroken run of twenty uppercase letters and digits that
# opens with it is redacted whether or not anyone issued it — and that is the
# answer rather than a fault in it, because such a run is a key's format
# exactly and nothing in the text tells the two apart. Sparing these would
# spare a real key written the same way.
#
# A space, a hyphen or a lowercase letter ends the run, so prose as it is
# ordinarily written is out of reach: the two cases below have to be written in
# unbroken capitals to fall this way, and the third is the same text with the
# spaces left in. The pattern's own file weighs the tightenings that were
# available and what each would have cost.

case: a word of twenty capitals opening with the temporary prefix
in:   ASIAPACIFICSOUTHEAST
out:  «aws-access-key-id»

case: a longer word of capitals loses the twenty a key would be
in:   ASIANELEPHANTCONSERVATION
out:  «aws-access-key-id»ATION

case: the same words with the spaces a reader would write
in:   ASIA PACIFIC SOUTHEAST and ASIAN ELEPHANT CONSERVATION
out:  ASIA PACIFIC SOUTHEAST and ASIAN ELEPHANT CONSERVATION

# And what this pattern leaves alone.
#
# The first three are the alphabet and the count. The rest are prefixes: IAM
# documents twelve, and the two above are the only two that name an access key
# ID. AIDA, AROA, AGPA, AIPA, ANPA, ANVA, APKA and ASCA are unique identifiers
# for a user, a role, a group, an instance profile, a policy, a policy version,
# a public key and a certificate: written into policy documents and CloudTrail
# records so that a reader can match one up, and authenticating nothing. Every
# one AWS shows is twenty-one characters rather than twenty, but AWS states no
# length for them either, so it is the prefix and not the count that keeps them
# out. ABIA and ACCA are credentials, a service bearer token and a
# context-specific credential, but AWS documents no shape for either beyond the
# prefix. AROA and ABIA stand for those two groups here.

case: a body one character too short
in:   AKIA0123456789ABCDE
out:  AKIA0123456789ABCDE

case: a lowercase body
in:   AKIA0123456789abcdef
out:  AKIA0123456789abcdef

case: a hyphen where the body would be
in:   AKIA-123456789ABCDEF
out:  AKIA-123456789ABCDEF

case: twenty uppercase characters that open with no prefix
in:   ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRST
out:  ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRST

case: a unique identifier for a role is not an access key id
in:   AROA0123456789ABCDEFG
out:  AROA0123456789ABCDEFG

case: a service bearer token has no documented shape
in:   ABIA0123456789ABCDEF
out:  ABIA0123456789ABCDEF

case: prose in capitals
in:   THERE IS NO CREDENTIAL IN THIS SENTENCE
out:  THERE IS NO CREDENTIAL IN THIS SENTENCE

# And the half of an AWS access key this library cannot reach. The secret
# access key is forty characters of base64 with no prefix and no length that
# tells it from any other forty, so nothing in the value says what it is and
# only the name written in front of it does, which no pattern here reads. It
# comes through whole on its own, and it comes through whole beside the key ID
# it belongs to — the case below is the pair as a credentials file holds it,
# and what is left in the text after masking is the secret and the name.

case: a secret access key on its own
in:   aws_secret_access_key = 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
out:  aws_secret_access_key = 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567

case: a secret access key beside the key id it belongs to
in:   [default]\naws_access_key_id = AKIA0123456789ABCDEF\naws_secret_access_key = 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
out:  [default]\naws_access_key_id = «aws-access-key-id»\naws_secret_access_key = 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567
